# Lazy-loaded rules

Rules in this directory are **not** eager-loaded into every Claude Code session. They live here until the system / milestone / topic they describe goes active — at which point they get promoted to `.claude/rules/` (eager) for the duration that work is hot, then demoted back here when the work is done.

## Why

Every line in `.claude/rules/` costs tokens **per session, every session**, whether or not the session touches that rule. Rules describing systems not yet under active implementation are net-negative — they crowd out hot rules and consume budget for content the model can't act on right now.

## Promotion / demotion criteria

A simple bucket model based on session-hit frequency:

| Bucket | Hit rate | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **HOT** | Hit in ≥ 3 of last 10 sessions | Keep in `.claude/rules/` |
| **WARM** | Hit in 1–2 of last 10 sessions | Keep eager IF foundational (architecture, input, settings); otherwise demote |
| **COLD** | Hit in 0 of last 10 sessions | Move to `docs/lazy/`, leave a one-line pointer in `CLAUDE.md` under "Lazy-loaded rules" |

When promoting back to eager: `git mv docs/lazy/<rule>.md .claude/rules/<rule>.md` + remove the pointer line from CLAUDE.md.

## How to point to a lazy rule from CLAUDE.md

In `CLAUDE.md`, under a "Lazy-loaded rules" section, list each with a one-line description:

```markdown
**Lazy-loaded rules** (fetch when the milestone goes active):
- `docs/lazy/<name>.md` — one-line summary of what it covers + when it becomes relevant
```

## Audit cadence

Re-run an audit at any of:

- **Every milestone transition** (M2 → M3, etc.). Rules cold in the previous milestone may go hot.
- **After any session where you notice rule bloat** ("Claude keeps reciting a rule we never touch").
- **Every ~10 new sessions** as a routine sanity check.

The audit script (if you build one) reads session transcripts and counts referenced hits per rule. A reference implementation lives at `tools/rules_audit/audit.py` in projects that built one.

---

## Lazy rules currently in this directory

(none yet — list them here as you demote them from `.claude/rules/`)

# Security posture: claude-code-templates

Internal record of what this project defends, which controls are live and which are owed. `.claude/rules/security.md` holds the everyday rule; this file holds the facts it points to. In a private repo, fill in the tables here, delete the rows that do not apply, and update the file at each review below.

In a public repo, fill in a copy kept somewhere private (a private repo, wiki or vault) and commit only this empty template: the open hardening items and the list of what is not defended map exactly where to attack.

## What we defend against

Rank the threats by expected loss, not by how alarming they sound. Common ones:

| Threat | Likelihood | What it costs us | Main control |
|---|---|---|---|
| An account that reaches the source or the release pipeline is taken over | | Full source, the ability to ship as us | Phishing-resistant two-factor sign-in, the inventory below |
| A secret ships in a build or the repo | | Whatever the secret opens | Secrets stay server-side; secret scanning |
| A shipped build is unpacked and read | | Readable code and assets | Nothing secret ships; the hardening list below |
| A build is repackaged and resold | | Sales, reputation | Trademark, takedown notices |
| A download or plugin carries a payload to users | | Users' machines and trust | Signed downloads, untrusted-input parsing |

## Credential inventory

Every door to the source, the build pipeline and the release channels. They are not one door: hardening one account leaves the others open.

| Door | What it opens | Where it lives | Who can read it | Rotation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Code host account | The repo, its history, CI secrets | | | |
| Cloud file sync of the working copy | The full working tree, `.git` included | | | |
| Store or publisher account | Shipping a build under our name | | | |
| CI secrets | Whatever each secret opens | | | |
| Developer machines | The working tree and cached sign-ins | | | |
| Third-party apps and access tokens | Whatever scope was granted | | | |

## Account hardening

- [ ] Phishing-resistant two-factor sign-in (security key or passkey) on every account in the inventory. SMS codes removed.
- [ ] Authorized third-party apps and access tokens reviewed; anything unused or unknown revoked.
- [ ] One backup behind a credential that none of the accounts above shares.
- [ ] A copyright notice at the repo root, so a takedown request has a dated claim to cite.

## What ships in each build

| Build | Contents | Who receives it | Readable by |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | Anyone who has it |

## Hardening at export

Each item filters casual extraction; none stops a determined reader.

- [ ] No debug symbols, source maps or internal logs in release builds.
- [ ] No `.env` files, test keys or sample credentials packed into a build.
- [ ] Internal strings (debug labels, assert messages) stripped where the toolchain allows.
- [ ] Builds that leave trusted hands (betas, demos, press) carry a mark that names the recipient.

## Downloads and plugins

Everything the app fetches or loads at run time, and how each is verified:

| What | From where | Verified by |
|---|---|---|
| | | |

## What we deliberately do not defend

Name what is not worth the cost (the concept, readable data meant for modders, determined reverse engineering), so effort goes where it pays.

## Review cadence

- At each milestone close: the inventory and the token review.
- Before any build leaves trusted hands: the export list.
- After any account compromise or near miss: at once, with what happened.

# Test-suite audit

How to check an existing suite against `.claude/rules/testing.md` § When a test earns its place. Run it when the suite feels slow or bloated, or once after adopting the rule. The aim is fewer tests with no loss of a guard a user would notice.

## Scan

List candidates per rule before judging any of them:

- **Near copies (rule 2):** tests in one file whose bodies are almost the same text.
- **Mutant checks (rule 4):** tests that rebuild an old or wrong version of a formula and assert it fails.
- **Seeded sweeps (rule 5):** tests that loop over random or generated input.
- **Benchmarks (rule 6):** tests that time code, or fail on a time budget.
- **Pinned internals (rule 3):** tests that assert a private constant, a size, a call count or a layout.

A short script that reads the test files is enough; keep it out of the repo.

## List A: mutant checks kept only when the old version was real

For each mutant check, find where it came from: `git log -S<test name> --reverse -- <test folder>` names the commit that first added it, even across file moves or splits.

- **Keep** it when it sits on a codec, fixed-point math or determinism, when it was added or later changed by a `fix` commit, or when the old version it rebuilds once shipped: search the source history for the line it removes.
- **Delete** it when the old version was invented: added in the same commit as the formula, or by a `feat`, `perf`, `refactor` or `test` commit, and never in the source.
- When in doubt, it stays. Record each borderline call and why.

The plain test the mutant paired with stays either way.

## List B: fold only tests of the same shape

Merge near copies into one table only when they make the same assertion on different input.

- Every row gets a name, so a failure says which case broke.
- Every row checks the whole outcome, never less than the tests it replaces. Folding often makes rows stricter.
- Keep tests apart when each guards a different function or path: a table would hide which one broke.
- Trace each old test to its row before deleting it.

## List C: keep sweeps that reach input no table can list

A seeded sweep stays when it covers input a boundary table cannot list (codecs, determinism, range invariants over a large space). It goes when a table already covers the same boundaries. Benchmarks move to their own command, outside the pass or fail suite.

## Landing the changes

- Small PRs, one list or one area at a time, each with the full suite green.
- Record the findings (counts per rule, what was deleted or folded, the borderline calls) in the PR body or a dated note, so the next audit starts from them.
- Checking rule 1 (does each test guard something a user would notice) means reading every test. Do it area by area, after the mechanical lists land.
